name: The Candler Oak

location.address: 516 Drayton Street, Savannah, GA (adjacent to Forsyth Park, on the former Candler Hospital / Savannah Law School site, now SCAD property)

access: Free. Viewable from the public sidewalk on Drayton Street; the tree's root zone is fenced off by the Savannah Tree Foundation to protect it from foot traffic and parking, so visitors view the tree from just outside the fence rather than approach the trunk itself.
transport: In Savannah's downtown Historic District, directly beside Forsyth Park; a walkable 15-20 minute stroll from the riverfront/City Market area, no dedicated parking at the site.
verify_notes: In 1984 (Wikipedia, citing the Georgia Urban Forest Council's 2001 Landmark and Historic Tree designation) the Savannah Tree Foundation secured what is described as the first conservation easement on a single tree in the US; the Foundation's own site gives the year as 1985. Easement size given as 6,804 linear feet by Wikipedia and 6,804 square feet by the Foundation's own page; kept both figures here rather than picking one. Age: Wikipedia gives both 'growing since the 1700s' and, separately, '350-450 years old' (mutually inconsistent framings); the Savannah Tree Foundation's own page, written by the org that has managed the tree for 45 years, says 'thought to be over 300 years old'. No girth-based growth-rate calculation found in either source; both figures read as inherited estimates rather than derived ones, and live oak ages are notoriously overstated (brief's own warning), so treat the top of the range with caution. Circumference 17 ft (518 cm) and diameter 63 in (160 cm) agree closely (pi x 160cm = 502cm, within rounding). Recovery story: when the easement was created, asphalt from an adjacent parking lot encircled the trunk and cars parked over the root system; arborists gave it 20 years to live. The Savannah Tree Foundation removed the asphalt, pruned and fenced it, and 45 years later reports it thriving. Individually named, single most documented tree in the city; strongest candidate in Savannah. Now on SCAD's Deloitte Foundry / former Savannah Law School property; the law school (2012) added its own fencing and camera surveillance before closing.

name: The Wormsloe Oak Avenue
age_estimate: roughly 130 years (the avenue itself, not the estate)

location.address: Wormsloe Historic Site, 7601 Skidaway Road, Savannah, GA 31406

access: Paid entry: $12 adults, $9 seniors (62+), $5.75 youth (6-17), $3.25 children under 6, plus tax. Open daily 9:00am to 4:45pm, closed Thanksgiving and Christmas Day. Managed by Georgia Department of Natural Resources as a State Historic Site.
transport: By car only, about 15-20 minutes southeast of downtown Savannah on the Isle of Hope; no meaningful public transit to the site.
verify_notes: BRIDGE CLAIM WARNING for the writer: Noble Jones founded Wormsloe Plantation in the 1730s alongside Oglethorpe, and the tabby house ruin there is the oldest standing structure in the Savannah area, but the famous mile-and-a-half oak avenue is NOT from that era. Two independent sources agree it was planted circa the early-to-late 1890s by Wymberley Jones De Renne, a Jones descendant (one source says to mark the birth of a 6th-generation descendant), with over 400 live oaks along a 1.5-mile (2.4km) dirt road. So the avenue is roughly 130-135 years old as of 2026, not colonial-era; do not let the plantation's founding date bleed into the oaks' age. Treated as one collectible entry per the ensemble rule: it is a single named, world-famous destination with one obvious place to stand (the avenue itself, entered from the visitor center), not a generic scatter of trees. No individual trunk girth or height found for any single tree in the avenue; do not invent one, the entry describes the avenue as a whole. Coordinates are the site's general location (Wikipedia infobox); the entrance/visitor-center end of the avenue is the practical 'stand here' point. Ownership: state-run since 1979, descendants of Noble Jones still hold ~50 acres around the family house nearby.
